question: Which statement best describes createContext?
options: A <Context.Provider value={...}> makes its value available to every descendant, and the nearest Provider above a consumer always wins over outer ones or the default. Nesting providers lets you override a value for a subtree. The critical gotcha is that passing a fresh object literal as value re-renders all consumers on every parent render, so the value should be memoized when it's an object.

createContext(defaultValue) builds a context object holding a Provider and (legacy) Consumer, and is typically defined at module scope so it can be imported anywhere. The default value is only a fallback for consumers rendered with no Provider above them. A common pattern is exporting both the context and a custom hook that wraps useContext to guard against missing providers.

The argument to createContext is returned by useContext only when there is no matching Provider anywhere above the consumer. With a Provider present, its value always takes precedence, so the default is mainly useful for isolated component tests and standalone usage. A common mistake is assuming consumers normally receive the default; in a real app wrapped in a Provider, they never do.

Prop drilling is threading a value through many intermediate components that don't use it, just to reach a deep consumer, which is verbose and fragile. Context solves this by letting any descendant read shared data directly, keeping middle components clean. The trade-off is that Context makes data flow less explicit, so it's best reserved for genuinely cross-cutting concerns like theme, auth, and locale rather than every shared prop.

options: Prop drilling is threading a value through many intermediate components that don't use it, just to reach a deep consumer, which is verbose and fragile. Every component calling useContext re-renders whenever the Provider's value changes, regardless of which field it reads, because Context has no selector mechanism. This means a broad context holding frequently-changing data can fan out re-renders across the tree. Memoizing the value and reading only what you need does not narrow this; the only real fix is splitting contexts or moving hot data elsewhere.

question: Which statement best describes Prop drilling?
options: When a Provider's value is an object built inline, it gets a new reference on every parent render, forcing all consumers to re-render even when nothing meaningful changed. Wrapping it in useMemo keyed on its real inputs keeps the reference stable across renders. This stops spurious re-renders from reference churn, though genuine value changes still propagate to all consumers.

Context distributes a value but has no batching, selectors, or middleware, so it is not a state-management library on its own. For complex global state with fine-grained subscriptions, external stores like Redux, Zustand, or useSyncExternalStore let components subscribe to a slice and re-render only when that slice changes. Context is often paired with useState/useReducer for simpler cases, and high-frequency data should avoid Context entirely.
